patterns.usage_note: Spoken contraction of ことは, so it appears wherever topicalized こと would: most often in the concessive frame 〜こた〜が (読んだこた読んだが) and in 〜こたない "there's no need to". It is casual and a little rough, common in male-sounding speech and in fiction dialogue. Anything written or polite uses the full ことは.

examples.ruby: 連絡[れんらく]するこたするが、期待[きたい]はしないでくれ。
examples.english: I'll get in touch, sure, but don't get your hopes up.

examples.ruby: 読[よ]んだこた読[よ]んだが、内容[ないよう]は覚[おぼ]えていない。
examples.english: Read it I did, but I don't remember a thing about it.

examples.ruby: 安[やす]いこた安[やす]いけど、すぐ壊[こわ]れそうだ。
examples.english: Cheap it certainly is, but it looks like it'll break right away.

glosses: … ing (turns a clause into a noun)
patterns.usage_note: Turns a clause into a noun, typically a concrete event the speaker sees, hears, or experiences, which is why verbs of perception take の, not こと (転ぶのを見た). Two sibling entries take the other jobs of this の: marking the subject of a noun-modifying clause in place of が (父の作った料理) and listing what someone is fussing about (暑いの寒いのと言う). こと is the abstract counterpart, required when the nominalization is the predicate (趣味は絵を描くことだ).

examples.ruby: 朝[あさ]早[はや]く起[お]きるのは本当[ほんとう]につらい。
examples.english: Getting up early in the morning is genuinely rough.

examples.ruby: 上[うえ]の階[かい]で誰[だれ]かがピアノを弾[ひ]いているのが聞[き]こえる。
examples.english: I can hear someone upstairs playing the piano.

examples.ruby: 弟[おとうと]が階段[かいだん]で転[ころ]ぶのを見[み]てしまった。
examples.english: I happened to see my little brother take a tumble on the stairs.
